questions.q: What is the biggest control-flow gap between T-SQL and almost every other language, including PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL?
options: T-SQL has no native FOR loop — WHILE plus a manually incremented counter is the only option
T-SQL cannot use IF statements at all
T-SQL has no way to print values
questions.explain: Unlike PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL, which both support FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP, T-SQL's idiom for a counting loop is WHILE with a manually declared and incremented counter variable.

questions.q: Which keyword do PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL use for 'else if' that T-SQL has no equivalent for?
questions.explain: PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL both use the one-word ELSIF keyword and close the whole statement with END IF; T-SQL has neither and wraps each branch in its own BEGIN/END instead.

questions.q: What loop construct does MySQL have that T-SQL and PL/SQL do not?
options: REPEAT...UNTIL, which checks its condition after the loop body runs
FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP, a native counting loop
WHILE...DO, which no other platform supports
questions.explain: MySQL's REPEAT...UNTIL...END REPEAT checks its condition after the body executes, guaranteeing at least one iteration, unlike a WHILE loop.

questions.q: Which keyword does MySQL use for 'else if', spelled differently from PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL's version?
questions.explain: MySQL spells it ELSEIF (one word), while PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL spell it ELSIF — a subtle but real difference that trips up developers moving between platforms.

questions.q: What must T-SQL wrap around a multi-statement IF or ELSE branch that the other three platforms don't require the same way?
options: A BEGIN...END block, since T-SQL has no END IF to close a whole multi-branch statement
questions.explain: T-SQL has no END IF — each branch that contains more than one statement needs its own BEGIN...END wrapper, unlike PL/SQL, MySQL, and PL/pgSQL which all close the entire IF with END IF.
